passage: The airport was roaring with cancelled-flight announcements, and Baljeet and Vikas had been stuck for three hours. When the cab fare home came up, Vikas snapped, "These cab drivers are all cheats." Baljeet was tired too and felt a flash of irritation, but kept the voice light. "Really? Mine this morning waited fifteen minutes at the gate and charged exactly the meter. Did something happen to you?" Vikas rubbed his neck. "One overcharged me last month, near the station." "That's rotten," Baljeet said. "Ever met a good one?" Vikas paused. "My regular driver, actually. He once drove my mother to hospital at night and refused a tip." "So he's not a cheat?" "No. I suppose not."

The office Diwali party was winding down when Alka, balancing a plate of samosas, said, "Honestly, these delivery boys from the hill towns are all thieves. Mine stole a parcel."
Sharmila put her glass down. "Oh no, which parcel?"
"Headphones. The tracking said delivered, and nothing came."
"That's awful. Did you find out who it was?"
"Well, no. But you know how they are."
"Hmm." Sharmila tilted her head. "The boy who brings my groceries is from Almora. Last month I left my wallet on the counter at the shop and he ran two lanes to give it back."
Alka paused. "Really?"
"Really. So I'm not sure it's about where they're from. Maybe it was one person. Or the parcel went to the wrong flat?"
Alka chewed slowly. "I didn't check with the neighbours, actually." She pulled out her phone. "Let me ask the building group."
Sharmila smiled and took a samosa.

qa.q: Where is the boy who brings Sharmila's groceries from?
qa.a: He is from Almora.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling when putting the glass down?
qa.a: Sharmila was probably uneasy and a little sad at the sweeping remark, yet calm enough to ask questions instead of arguing.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila's approach work better than attacking Alka?
qa.a: She asked questions and gave a personal example, so Alka could doubt the label herself without feeling shamed in front of colleagues.

qa.q: How might Alka see the lost parcel after the conversation?
qa.a: Alka seems less sure it was about where the delivery boys come from, and more open to checking what actually happened.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who meets a sweeping remark with questions and a personal example, keeping the other person's dignity and planting doubt.

It's been a few months, so I can tell this one properly. We were at Dhruv's birthday dinner, eight of us round a table at the dhaba, and Dhruv said, "Girls from small towns can't handle big-city jobs. They crack in six months." Some laughed. I felt my jaw tighten. My sister is from exactly that kind of town, our town, and she runs a hospital billing team in Mumbai.
I wanted to say, "That's a stupid thing to say." I didn't. I asked, "Who have you seen crack?" He thought. "My cousin's friend, I think." Then I said, "My sister moved from Jhansi at twenty-two. She's a team lead now." Dhruv blinked. "Really? That's cool." A month later, he messaged me. His office was hiring from a small-town college, and he'd pushed for one of them. "Your sister's fault," he wrote. I, Sachin, have that screenshot saved.

qa.q: Where did Sachin's sister move from?
qa.a: She moved from Jhansi at twenty-two.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel when Dhruv made the remark?
qa.a: Sachin felt angry, with a tight jaw, because the remark insulted people like Sachin's own sister.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking "Who have you seen crack?" and sharing the sister's story, instead of calling the remark stupid, let Dhruv keep his dignity and actually rethink it.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt when he heard about Sachin's sister?
qa.a: Dhruv seemed surprised and interested rather than defensive, which left room for him to change his view later.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who answers a sweeping remark with a question and a personal example, keeping dignity safe and planting a real doubt.

Team lead's note, content team, after Thursday's hiring review.
During the shortlist discussion, Shalini said, "Let's skip the government-school candidates. They can't write proper English." A couple of people nodded. I was about to step in when Kavitha, our newest writer, spoke up. She didn't sound angry. She said, "Can I ask what you've seen that makes you think that?" Shalini said it was just common knowledge. Kavitha smiled a little and said, "I went to a government school in Madurai. My first English teacher had only one textbook for forty of us. I think I write alright." The room went quiet. Shalini looked embarrassed, then laughed and said, "You write better than me." Kavitha laughed too, and nobody was shamed.
We agreed to judge only the writing test. After the meeting Shalini asked Kavitha to review her own blog. I have noted Kavitha's handling for her next appraisal.

qa.q: Where did Kavitha go to school?
qa.a: A government school in Madurai.

qa.q: What was Shalini likely feeling when the room went quiet?
qa.a: Shalini was probably embarrassed, caught out by a real example that contradicted her remark.

qa.q: What did Kavitha's reply do well?
qa.a: It asked a genuine question and offered a personal story without anger, so Shalini could change her mind without being humiliated.

qa.q: How might the government-school candidates be affected by the change in the meeting?
qa.a: They would now be judged on their actual writing test rather than being skipped because of a label.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who challenges a sweeping remark with a question and personal example, keeping dignity safe so the other person rethinks.

Tuesday, late.
Lunch at the office today. Gurleen was sorting the new interns for the client project and said, loud enough for the whole table, "Not the ones from government schools, their English falls apart on calls." Two people nodded. My face went hot. First instinct: slam my tiffin down and call her a snob.
I didn't. I asked, "What makes you say that? Was there a call that went badly?" She said not really, it's just known. So I said, "I did Class 1 to 12 in a government school in Nanded. I've handled the Singapore client for a year now." She stared at me. "Seriously? I'd never have guessed."
At five she stopped by my desk and asked which intern I'd pick. I said Farhan. She put him on the list.
One lunch probably changes nothing big. But she looked like she was actually thinking, not defending. Shouting would never have got me that.
— Chaitanya

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya study from Class 1 to 12?
qa.a: In a government school in Nanded.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's hot face at lunch suggest?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt angry and insulted, even tempted to slam the tiffin and call Gurleen a snob, but chose to hold that anger back and ask instead.

qa.q: Why did a question and a personal example work better than an attack?
qa.a: They kept Gurleen's dignity safe, so she could think instead of defend herself, and the example planted a real doubt; by five she was asking which intern to pick.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt on learning where Chaitanya studied?
qa.a: She was surprised and perhaps a little embarrassed, and her visit to the desk shows her fixed idea had started to wobble.
